content: The metre, symbolized as m, is the fundamental unit of length in the International System of Units (SI). Initially, it was defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the Earth's equator to the North Pole along a meridian. However, the modern definition of the metre is based on the speed of light, specifically as the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. This definition ties the metre to a universal constant, ensuring its precision and reproducibility. As the base unit of length in the SI system, all other SI units involving length, such as area (square metres) or speed (metres per second), are derived from the metre. Decimal multiples and submultiples of the metre, such as the kilometre (1,000 metres) and centimetre (0.01 metres), are created by applying SI prefixes. Its first recorded use in English to denote this unit of length dates back to 1797. Historical Definitions of the Metre Meridional Definition In the 18th century, two primary proposals were considered for defining the standard unit of length. One suggested using the length of a pendulum with a half-period of one second, while the other proposed defining the metre as one ten-millionth of the Earth's meridian length from the equator to the North Pole. In 1791, the French Academy of Sciences adopted the meridional definition. Based on provisional results, France adopted the metre as its official unit of length in 1793. Although later calculations revealed a slight error in the prototype metre bar due to an incorrect estimation of the Earth's flattening, this length became the standard. The Earth's polar circumference was thus approximated to be 40 million metres. Prototype Metre Bar In the 1870s, international conferences were held to establish new metric standards. This organization was tasked with preserving the new prototype metre and kilogram standards, distributing national prototypes, and maintaining consistency with non-metric standards. In 1960, the eleventh CGPM redefined the metre in terms of the wavelength of light, specifically as 1,650,763.73 wavelengths of the orange-red emission line of krypton-86 in a vacuum. This marked the transition from a physical prototype to a definition based on atomic properties. Helium-Neon Laser Wavelength Standard To further enhance precision, the seventeenth CGPM in 1983 redefined the metre based on the speed of light. The metre was now defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second. This definition also fixed the speed of light in a vacuum at exactly 299,792,458 metres per second. While the metre is defined in terms of time and the speed of light, its practical realization in laboratories involves counting wavelengths of light over a given distance. The iodine-stabilized helium-neon laser was recommended as a standard radiation source for this purpose. The wavelength of the helium-neon laser is currently defined as 632.99139822 nanometres, with a relative standard uncertainty of 2.5 × 10⁻¹¹. This uncertainty is the limiting factor in laboratory realizations of the metre, as it is significantly less precise than the definition of the second. Timeline of Metre Definitions 1790 (May 8): The French National Assembly proposed defining the metre as the length of a pendulum with a half-period of one second. 1791 (March 30): The French Academy of Sciences recommended defining the metre as one ten-millionth of the Earth's meridian length from the equator to the North Pole. 1795: A provisional metre bar made of brass was constructed. 1799 (December 10): A platinum metre bar was adopted as the final standard and deposited in the French National Archives. 1889 (September 28): The first CGPM defined the metre as the distance between two lines on a platinum-iridium bar at 0°C. 1927 (October 6): The seventh CGPM refined the definition to specify the distance between the axes of two central lines on the prototype bar under specific conditions. 1960 (October 20): The eleventh CGPM redefined the metre as 1,650,763.73 wavelengths of krypton-86 radiation in a vacuum. 1983 (October 21): The seventeenth CGPM redefined the metre as the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second.
